title: What Is an RFI? A Clear Guide to Request for Information, With Examples
summary: An RFI is a request for information. See how buyers use RFIs to research vendors, how construction RFIs differ, and how vendors should respond.
body_markdown:
An RFI is a request for information. It is a formal document one party sends another to gather facts before making a decision. The abbreviation carries two distinct meanings in US business, and they belong to different processes:


- **In procurement** , a buyer issues an RFI to potential vendors early in the sourcing process, before any proposal or pricing request, to learn what solutions exist and which suppliers are capable.
- **In construction** , a contractor submits an RFI to the architect, engineer, or owner during a project to clarify drawings, specifications, or site conditions.


This guide explains both. It also covers what belongs in an RFI, how RFI differs from RFP and RFQ, and how vendors should decide whether and how to respond.


### **Key Takeaways**


- An RFI (request for information) is a document used to gather facts before a decision. It has two common uses:[procurement](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/procurement-rfis-request-for-information) and construction.
- In procurement, a buyer sends an RFI to vendors early, before an RFP or RFQ, to learn what solutions and suppliers exist.
- In construction, a contractor sends an RFI to the design team to clarify drawings, specs, or site conditions during a project.
- An RFI is not a bid and is not binding. Responding creates no obligation, and no award follows directly from it.
- In the sourcing sequence, an RFI comes before the[RFP](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/what-is-a-request-for-proposal-rfp) (full proposal) and the RFQ (firm pricing).


## RFI in Procurement: The Buyer's Research Document


A procurement RFI is market research in document form. The buyer knows it has a problem but does not yet know the full range of solutions, the capable suppliers, or sometimes even the right requirements. So it asks the market before it asks for proposals.


A well-built RFI requests facts a buyer can compare: company background, relevant experience, solution capabilities, compliance credentials such as SOC 2 or ISO certifications, integration options, and implementation approach. It does not request detailed pricing or a full proposed solution. Those belong to the RFQ and RFP stages that may follow.


### What happens after an RFI


The buyer compares responses, refines its requirements based on what it learned, and typically shortlists vendors for the next stage. Three outcomes are common:


1. **An**[RFP](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/rfp-request-for-proposal-your-ultimate-guide-to-rfps) **follows.** The buyer now understands the market and asks shortlisted vendors for full proposals.
2. **An RFQ follows.** The buyer's requirement turned out to be a defined product or service, so it goes straight to pricing.
3. **Nothing follows.** The research showed the project is premature, too expensive, or already solved internally. This outcome is normal, and vendors should factor it into how much effort a response deserves.

## RFI in Construction: How Contractors Get Answers On-Site


A construction RFI works differently. It is a formal, logged question from the contractor to the design team when the drawings, specifications, or site conditions leave something unclear, missing, or contradictory. The answer becomes part of the project record, and if it changes cost or schedule, it can trigger a change order.


The volume is larger than most people outside the industry expect. The widely cited[Navigant Construction Forum study](https://www.cmaanet.org/sites/default/files/2018-04/NCF%20IMPACT%20%26%20CONTROL%20OF%20RFIs%20ON%20CONSTRUCTION%20PROJECTS.pdf) of 1,362 projects and more than one million RFIs found an average of 796 RFIs per project, an average cost of about $1,080 to review and respond to each one, and an average first reply time of 6.4 days. On a typical project, that adds up to hundreds of thousands of dollars in administrative cost, which is why construction teams invest in RFI logs, standard formats, and response deadlines.


A good construction RFI states the exact location, references the specific drawing or spec section, asks one clear question, and proposes a solution the designer can confirm or reject. Our overview of the[different types of construction RFIs](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/different-types-rfi-construction) breaks down the main categories.


## Key Components of an RFI and How Issuers Write One


### The components


A complete RFI contains seven parts:


1. **Basic request details.** Issuer name, RFI title and reference number, issue date, response deadline, and a contact for questions.
2. **Statement of purpose.** What decision the information will support and why the organization is going to market now.
3. **Company background.** A short profile of the issuer so vendors can tailor their responses to the size and industry involved.
4. **Project summary and scope.** The problem, the current environment, known constraints, and the approximate scale.
5. **Information requested.** Structured questions covering company profile, relevant experience, solution capabilities, compliance credentials, integration options, implementation approach, and pricing model. Each question should map to something the buyer will evaluate.
6. **Response instructions.** Format, submission method, page limit, and deadline. A standard response template keeps answers comparable.
7. **Next steps.** What follows the RFI, and when respondents will hear back.


### The writing process, step by step


1. **Define the decision first.** Write down what you need to decide after reading the responses. Every question earns its place by serving that decision.
2. **Draft the seven components** , keeping the question list short. Twenty focused questions produce better responses than fifty broad ones.
3. **Prescreen the distribution list.** Sending an RFI to every vendor in the category produces a pile of responses nobody can process. Target vendors that plausibly fit.
4. **Send it with a response template and a realistic deadline.** Two to three weeks is a reasonable floor for a substantive RFI.
5. **Evaluate consistently and close the loop.** Score responses against the same criteria, notify respondents of the outcome, and record what you learned for the RFP stage.


A ready-made structure speeds this up. Our[RFI template](https://www.inventive.ai/blog-posts/rfi-template-word) provides the full document skeleton.


## RFI Example


Here is a condensed procurement RFI that shows the components in use.


Request for Information: Customer Support Platform


Issued by:


Regional insurance provider, ~2,000 employees | RFI-2026-014 | Responses due: 3 weeks from issue


Purpose:


We are researching cloud customer support platforms for three call centers with roughly 400 agents, replacing a legacy on-premise system. Responses will inform an RFP planned for next quarter.


Scope specifics:


Cloud deployment required. Must integrate with Salesforce and our existing telephony system. HIPAA compliance is mandatory. Rollout would be phased across three sites.


Information requested:


Company profile and years in market. Platform capabilities against the scope above. Compliance certifications with audit dates. Integration approach for the named systems. Typical implementation timeline for a deployment of this size. Pricing model (a description of how you charge, not a quote).


Response instructions:


Maximum 10 pages, submitted through the portal linked below. Questions by email during week one; answers will be shared with all recipients.


Next steps:


Shortlisted vendors will be notified within two weeks of the deadline and invited to the RFP.
